chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah, from his father, from Khalaf ibn Hammad, from Saeed al-Naqqash, who said:

Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Indeed, in Al-Fitr there is Takbeer, but it is concealed.' I said, 'And where is it?' He said: 'On the night of Al-Fitr, during Maghrib and the last Isha, and in the Fajr prayer, and in the Eid prayer. Then it is cut off.'

I said, 'How should I say it?' He said: 'You should say: Allah is the Greatest, Allah is the Greatest, There is no god except Allah, and Allah is the Greatest, Allah is the Greatest, and to Allah belongs the praise, Allah is the Greatest for what He guided us.' And this is the Word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'And to make complete the period [of fasting] and to magnify Allah for that He has guided you.'
A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn Asbaat, from Khalaf ibn Hammad — similar to it.

key_terms.الْفِطْرِ: Eid al-Fitr (Festival of Breaking the Fast)
key_terms.تَكْبِيراً: Takbeer (Exalming Allah by saying 'Allah is the Greatest')
key_terms.مَسْتُورٌ: Concealed (referring to reciting quietly or individually rather than aloud in congregation)

ai.seo_question: What is the specific time and formula for reciting Takbeer on the night of Eid al-Fitr according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the specific protocol for the concealed Takbeer during the night and day of Eid al-Fitr, emphasizing its recitation during Maghrib, Isha, Fajr, and the Eid prayer itself. It provides the precise formula—'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, La ilaha illa Allahu, wa Allahu Akbar, wa lillahi al-hamd'—and explicitly links it to the Quranic command to magnify Allah for guidance, reinforcing the Shia practice of integrating liturgical praise with scriptural injunctions.
